clue.text: Whig can disguise conversation

indicators.note: to disguise something is to alter its appearance, so these letters are rearranged into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Whig politician is able to hide behind idle chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disguise' looks like a verb with 'conversation' as its object, but it tells you to shuffle WHIG and CAN together.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosy natter or gossip session is informally called a chinwag in British English.

clue.text: Constellation once an ugly duckling

definitions.meaning: a northern star group named after the Latin word for swan
in Hans Christian Andersen's tale the ugly duckling grows up into a swan, and the Latin for swan is this word

explanation.surface: A star pattern in the sky was formerly an unlovely young bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Cygnus is both the Swan constellation and the Latin word for swan, the bird the ugly duckling became.

clue.text: To repeat after student is scholarly

indicators.note: the answer, put after the student's letter, would make the word for scholarly; so remove that letter from the front

parts.note: a scholarly person is literate, well read and educated
L is the learner, a student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A pupil repeats lessons and so becomes learned.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'to repeat, coming after student, is scholarly': L before the answer makes LITERATE, so the answer is LITERATE without L.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to do or say something again, a formal synonym for repeating.

clue.text: One of those spun by Porter?

definitions.text: One of those spun by Porter?

parts.words: One of those spun by Porter?
parts.note: William Sydney Porter, who wrote as O. Henry, published a story collection whose title is the plural of this word; stories are 'spun' like yarns, and the toy itself is spun

explanation.surface: A question about something a porter twirls round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porter' looks like a hotel porter or the drink; it is the real surname of O. Henry, whose 1910 collection was 'Whirligigs'.
explanation.definitionFit: A whirligig is a spinning toy or top, and also the title word of O. Henry's tales.

clue.text: A fairly glum absurd medley

indicators.note: absurd means ridiculous and out of order, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rather gloomy, ridiculous mixture of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absurd' tells you to rearrange A, FAIRLY and GLUM, eleven letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallimaufry is a confused jumble or hotchpotch, a mixed assortment like a medley.

clue.text: Browning wrote of his Italian touch

definitions.text: Browning wrote of his Italian touch

parts.words: Browning wrote of his Italian touch
parts.note: Robert Browning's poem 'A Toccata of ...' names this Venetian composer; toccata comes from the Italian for 'touch'

explanation.surface: The poet Browning described an Italian's deft touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touch' translates toccata, so the clue points to Browning's poem 'A Toccata of Galuppi's', about the 18th-century Venetian composer Baldassare Galuppi.
explanation.definitionFit: Baldassare Galuppi was the Venetian composer whose toccata Browning's poem concerns.

clue.text: Good American character of Eliot

parts.note: US stands for the United States, so American

explanation.surface: A decent American figure created by the poet Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: In T. S. Eliot's 'Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats', Gus is the Theatre Cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Gus, the Theatre Cat, is one of T. S. Eliot's feline creations in Old Possum.

clue.text: Snake-woman in Austin's cold-weather billet

annotationWithheld.why: Snake-woman in Austin's cold-weather billet (5): LAMIA is Keats's snake-woman, but no reading of 'in Austin's cold-weather billet' could be found as wordplay or a second definition; the reference may be misread from the page

clue.text: Shepherdess whose name was lost

parts.note: in Shakespeare's 'The Winter's Tale' the abandoned princess raised as a shepherdess has a Latin name meaning 'lost one'

explanation.surface: A country girl who has forgotten what she is called.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin perdita means 'lost', the name Antigonus gives the baby he abandons in 'The Winter's Tale'.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdita, the lost daughter of Leontes, is brought up as a shepherdess in Bohemia.

clue.text: Brand new dramatic style, perhaps

parts.note: 'Brand' is the title of a verse play by the Norwegian dramatist Henrik Ibsen, so a new style of drama like his is named after him

explanation.surface: A completely fresh theatrical manner, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand new' reads as 'completely new', but Brand is Ibsen's 1865 play.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibsenism is the realist, socially probing manner of Ibsen's plays, the new drama of the 1880s and 1890s.

clue.text: Some irregular characters (irregularly arranged?) of V. S. Naipaul

definitions.text: Some irregular characters (irregularly arranged?) of V. S. Naipaul

parts.words: Some irregular characters (irregularly arranged?) of V. S. Naipaul
parts.note: Naipaul's 1975 novel is about irregular fighters; the bracket hints that the title's letters are spelt in an irregular way here

explanation.surface: Odd figures, perhaps oddly ordered, in a Naipaul book.
explanation.walkthrough: Naipaul's novel is 'Guerrillas', with a double R; the grid's one-R spelling is the variant the bracketed question admits.
explanation.definitionFit: Guerillas are irregular soldiers, the subject and title of Naipaul's novel set in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Margaret Atwood provides an alias for this miss

definitions.text: Margaret Atwood provides an alias for this miss

parts.words: Margaret Atwood provides an alias for this miss
parts.note: Atwood's novel 'Alias Grace' gives the first name of its heroine, the real-life Canadian servant Grace, so her surname is wanted

explanation.surface: A novelist supplies a pseudonym for a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an alias' points to Atwood's title 'Alias Grace'; its heroine, Miss Grace Marks, was convicted of murder in 1843.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace Marks is the historical servant girl at the centre of Atwood's 'Alias Grace'.

clue.text: First university demolished entirely for dramatist

indicators.note: First applies to each of the two words after it, taking the opening letter of both

parts.note: entirely means wholly, all of it

explanation.surface: A campus is the first to be razed completely for the sake of a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Udall wrote 'Ralph Roister Doister', often called the first English comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Udall was the Tudor schoolmaster and playwright of 'Ralph Roister Doister'.

clue.text: Impression made by Lowell

parts.note: Robert Lowell's 1961 book of free translations of European poets is titled with the plural of a word for an impression or copy

explanation.surface: The effect the poet Lowell had on people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impression' suggests an effect made; it is a mimicking impression, and Lowell's book is 'Imitations'.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitation is a copy or impersonation, the sense in which a mimic does impressions.

clue.text: Elect to French Academy

parts.note: members of the Academie francaise are nicknamed 'les immortels', so electing someone to it makes them one of the undying

explanation.surface: Vote someone into the French Academy.
explanation.walkthrough: The forty members of the Academie francaise are called 'the immortals'.
explanation.definitionFit: To immortalise is to make undying or everlasting, as the Academy's nickname for members implies.

clue.text: Young Germans who produced a hypothesis of sound change

definitions.text: Young Germans who produced a hypothesis of sound change

parts.words: Young Germans who produced a hypothesis of sound change
parts.note: the Leipzig 'Junggrammatiker' of the 1870s held that sound laws admit no exceptions; their German name literally means young grammarians

explanation.surface: Youthful Germans who proposed a theory about how sounds shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young' renders the Jung- of Junggrammatiker, the linguists Brugmann, Osthoff and others.
explanation.definitionFit: The Neogrammarians were the 19th-century German linguists who proposed exceptionless sound laws.

clue.text: Nabokov showed preference for this parliamentarian…

definitions.text: Nabokov showed preference for this parliamentarian…

parts.words: Nabokov showed preference for this parliamentarian
parts.note: the clue pairs with the next one: Nabokov favoured ... people over the egg-headed, and a parliamentarian of the English Civil War was a puritan with cropped hair

explanation.surface: Nabokov preferred one member of parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Civil War, supporters of Parliament were called Roundheads for their close-cropped hair; the clue runs on into 16 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundheads were the Parliamentarian side in the English Civil War, named for their short haircuts.

clue.text: … and felt these were terrible philistines

definitions.text: … and felt these were terrible philistines

parts.words: and felt these were terrible philistines
parts.note: continuing from 15 down, Nabokov thought pretentious intellectuals were awful philistines, a joke since highbrows are supposedly the opposite of philistines

explanation.surface: He also thought certain people were dreadful boors.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox is the point: intellectuals are meant to be the enemies of philistinism, yet Nabokov scorned them as such.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggheads are highbrow intellectuals, the bookish types opposed in theory to philistines.

clue.text: His production was inconstant

parts.note: the Irish dramatist's 1702 comedy is titled 'The Inconstant', so his production, or play, was that

explanation.surface: His output was erratic and unreliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inconstant' reads as a verdict on his work, but 'The Inconstant' is the title of one of Farquhar's comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: George Farquhar, author of 'The Recruiting Officer', also wrote the comedy 'The Inconstant'.

clue.text: Decapitated dream god as bereaved poet

indicators.note: decapitated means with the head cut off, so the first letter of the dream god goes

parts.note: Morpheus is the Greek god of dreams

explanation.surface: A headless god of sleep appears as a grieving poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Orpheus lost his wife Eurydice and was himself beheaded by the Maenads, so the surface fits too.
explanation.definitionFit: Orpheus, the mythical singer and poet, lost his wife Eurydice to the underworld.

clue.text: Hornung's cracksman presumably unrewarded

parts.note: E. W. Hornung's gentleman thief Raffles appears in 'The ... Cracksman', and the missing title word describes someone who is not paid

explanation.surface: A safebreaker in Hornung's stories probably went unpaid.
explanation.walkthrough: Hornung's first Raffles book is 'The Amateur Cracksman' (1899); an amateur is, by definition, unpaid.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur does something for love rather than payment, hence unrewarded.

clue.text: Poet depicts lowland with extremes of reality

parts.note: a vale is a valley, low-lying land

indicators.note: extremes of means the first and last letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A poet portrays a valley with the outer edges of reality.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Valery was the French poet of 'Le Cimetiere marin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Valery was a major French Symbolist poet and essayist.

clue.text: Flute played at her nuptials

parts.note: in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' Francis Flute the bellows-mender acts Thisbe in the play staged for the wedding of Theseus and the Amazon queen

explanation.surface: A flute was played at a woman's wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flute' looks like an instrument; it is the rude mechanical who plays Thisbe at the Duke's wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, marries Theseus at the close of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.

clue.text: Make speech in part of actor at Elsinore

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A player at Hamlet's castle declaims a role.
explanation.walkthrough: Elsinore is Hamlet's castle, where the travelling players perform.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal address, especially a pompous one.

clue.text: Drink before a play

indicators.note: before puts the drink ahead of the letter that follows it

parts.note: a dram is a small measure of whisky

explanation.surface: Having a drink before going to the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama is a work for the stage, a synonym for a play.

clue.text: Borges booked the venue, it seems

definitions.text: Borges booked the venue, it seems

parts.words: Borges booked the venue, it seems
parts.note: Borges wrote 'El libro de ...', The Book of Sand, and the Spanish word for sand is also the English word for a stadium

explanation.surface: Borges reserved the location, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booked' means 'put in a book title', not 'reserved': Borges's 'The Book of Sand' is 'El libro de arena' in Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a sports or entertainment venue, and the word is Latin and Spanish for sand.

clue.text: Gather round table revealing her marriage gift

definitions.text: Gather round table revealing her marriage gift

parts.words: Gather round table revealing her marriage gift
parts.note: in Malory and Tennyson, King Leodegrance gives the Round Table to Arthur as the dowry of his daughter, Arthur's queen

explanation.surface: Assemble at the table to unwrap a wedding present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round table' looks like a meal setting; in the legends the Round Table was Arthur's queen's dowry.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinevere, Arthur's queen, brought the Round Table to Camelot as her wedding portion.

clue.text: Neon, possibly, on McGinty's house

parts.note: neon is an example of a noble element of this state, and the word placed before 'house' gives the '... House' of the McGinty in the old song and its nickname

explanation.surface: Perhaps a neon sign hangs on McGinty's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neon' looks like lighting on a building; it is an example of a gas, and 'Gas House' is a nickname tied to McGinty.
explanation.definitionFit: Neon is one of the noble gases, so a gas is what it is.

clue.text: Swinburne's siblings

parts.note: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote a verse tragedy titled 'The ...', after the female siblings at its heart

explanation.surface: The poet Swinburne's brothers and sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Swinburne's 1892 play is 'The Sisters'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisters are female siblings, and the word is also the title of Swinburne's drama.

clue.text: Joseph Kell's outside man, alias Piggy Hogg

definitions.text: Joseph Kell's outside man, alias Piggy Hogg

parts.words: Joseph Kell's outside man, alias Piggy Hogg
parts.note: Anthony Burgess, writing as Joseph Kell, created a flatulent poet who appears in 'Inside Mr ...' and 'The Clockwork Testament', and who takes the name Piggy Hogg

explanation.surface: A pen name's outsider, also known as Piggy Hogg.
explanation.walkthrough: Burgess published 'Inside Mr Enderby' as Joseph Kell; a later novel is 'Enderby Outside', where the poet lives as the barman Piggy Hogg.
explanation.definitionFit: F. X. Enderby is Burgess's lavatory-bound poet, who hides under the name Hogg.
